name: Peregrine Mission One
operator: Astrobotic (US, commercial, flying NASA CLPS payloads)
short_status: Launched Jan 8, 2024 on Vulcan's first flight; a helium-valve failure hours later ruled out landing; controlled South Pacific reentry Jan 18, 2024.
tagline: Astrobotic · United States · Lander · 2024 · Commercial and multipolar Failure
stats: in space, launch to controlled reentry
NASA CLPS task order (5 science payloads)

facts.label: Organisations
facts.value: Astrobotic (US, commercial, flying NASA CLPS payloads)

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 8 January 2024, 07:18 UTC (2:18 a.m. EST), Cape Canaveral SLC-41

facts.label: Launch vehicle
facts.value: ULA Vulcan Centaur VC2S, maiden flight (Cert-1)

facts.label: Failure cause
facts.value: Helium pressure control valve PCV2 failed to reseal during propulsion commissioning; oxidizer tank 'Tank 5' over-pressurized and ruptured

facts.label: Root cause (review board)
facts.value: Vibration-initiated relaxation of threaded components inside the valve, replicated in ground testing; 34-member board chaired by Dr. John Horack (Ohio State)

facts.label: End of mission
facts.value: Controlled reentry over the South Pacific, 18 January 2024, ~21:04 UTC (4:04 p.m. EST), after 10 days 14 hours and 535,000+ miles

facts.label: NASA payloads
facts.value: 5 under task order TO2-AB (LRA, NSS, LETS, NIRVSS, PITMS); 4 of 5 collected data in flight (LRA is passive)

facts.label: NASA task order value
facts.value: About $108 million (up from the initial $79.5 million award, for 5 payloads instead of 14)

facts.label: Total manifest
facts.value: 20 payloads from seven nations and 16 commercial customers

facts.label: Intended landing
facts.value: Sinus Viscositatis, adjacent to the Gruithuisen Domes; touchdown planned 23 February 2024, ~10 Earth days of surface ops

facts.label: Lander dimensions
facts.value: ~1.9 m tall, ~2.5 m across, 90 kg payload capacity, five TALOS-150 thrusters (MMH/MON-25)

facts.label: Human-remains controversy
facts.value: Celestis and Elysium Space memorial capsules drew a formal objection from Navajo Nation President Buu Nygren and a White House-convened meeting days before launch

facts.label: What came next
facts.value: Griffin Mission One targeted NET November 2026 (as of 13 July 2026); Astrobotic acquired by Voyager Technologies in 2026, now Voyager Lunar Systems; Peregrine-2 planned for 2028 under a $298M CLPS task order

timeline: Liftoff at 07:18 UTC on the maiden Vulcan Centaur: first CLPS launch, first US commercial lunar lander launch
Avionics and power up at 08:16 UTC; communications established via NASA's Deep Space Network
PCV2 fails to reseal during propulsion pressurization, hours into the mission; oxidizer Tank 5 ruptures and leaks; soft landing ruled out
Team stabilizes spacecraft; 4 of 5 NASA instruments plus other payloads collect data in cislunar space; 8 potentially mission-ending anomalies handled
Astrobotic, consulting NASA, decides on controlled Earth reentry to avoid debris risk in cislunar space
Controlled reentry over open water in the South Pacific at ~21:04 UTC; mission ends
Post-mission report published: root cause confirmed as vibration-loosened threaded joint in PCV2; corrective valve redesign for future landers
Successor lander Griffin-1 unveiled ahead of environmental testing; launch targeted NET November 2026 (as of Jul 13, 2026)
Voyager Technologies completes Astrobotic acquisition (now Voyager Lunar Systems); $298M CLPS award includes Peregrine-2, planned 2028, to the Gruithuisen Domes
